title: Pressure-cooker chicken risotto
subtitle: Creamy risotto without the 25 minutes of stirring
excerpt: A proper, creamy risotto cooked under pressure in 8 minutes. Chicken thighs, arborio rice, and stock go in together; the result is indistinguishable from the stovetop version.
sourceNotes: Risotto is a northern Italian staple, documented in recipes from Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina e l'Arte di Mangiare Bene (1891). The pressure-cooker method was popularised in the 1990s as a practical adaptation of the traditional stirred method.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Risotto does not hold well. Cook and serve immediately. Leftovers can be made into arancini.

content.text: Pressure-cooker chicken risotto is the weeknight shortcut that actually delivers. The rice cooks in the chicken stock under pressure for 8 minutes, absorbing the liquid and releasing starch in the same way as the traditional stirred method, but without the constant attention. The result is a creamy, cohesive risotto rather than a thick chicken soup.

Arborio rice is the right choice here. The short, starchy grain holds together under pressure better than basmati or long-grain rice, which turn mushy. Toast the rice briefly in the pot before adding the stock, this step keeps the grains separate.
Stir in the cold butter and Parmesan at the end, off the heat. This is the mantecatura, the final emulsification that makes risotto creamy rather than just wet. Do it vigorously.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté (or use the open pot on the hob). Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 4 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} of sliced garlic and the chicken pieces. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 minutes until the chicken is no longer pink on the outside.
Add {{arborio-rice}} of arborio rice to the pot. Stir for 1 minute until the grains look slightly translucent at the edges. This toasting step keeps them from becoming mushy under pressure.

Pour in {{stock-chicken}} of hot chicken stock. Stir once to deglaze the base of the pot. Season with salt and pepper. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 8 minutes. Quick-release the pressure.

Open the lid. The risotto will look slightly soupy, this is correct. Add the cold {{unsalted-butter}} of diced butter and {{parmesan}} of grated Parmesan. Stir vigorously for 1 to 2 minutes until the risotto comes together and turns creamy. Serve immediately.

rows.cause: The cooking time was too long, or the rice was not arborio. Long-grain rice overcooks quickly under pressure.
rows.fix: Use arborio or carnaroli rice only. Reduce the pressure-cook time to 7 minutes if your cooker runs hot. Serve immediately, risotto continues cooking in its own heat.

rows.cause: The pot was opened too soon, or insufficient starch was released from the rice.
rows.fix: Set the open pot on the hob over medium heat for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the excess liquid is absorbed. Add the butter and Parmesan after.

rows.symptom: The rice is undercooked in the centre
rows.cause: The pressure was not fully reached, or the cooking time was too short.
rows.fix: Return the sealed pot to high pressure and cook for a further 2 minutes. Quick-release again and finish with butter and cheese.

rows.cause: The stock was under-seasoned, or the Parmesan quantity was too small.
rows.fix: Season generously at the end, salt, pepper, and additional Parmesan will lift the flavour considerably. Good stock is what carries this dish.

content.text: Risotto has a reputation for demanding constant presence, the ladle, the stir, the gradual addition of hot stock. The pressure cooker version collapses that process into a 10-minute active period, producing something that would pass unremarked in a straightforward midweek dinner. The chicken pieces stay tender and the rice creamy. It is a good entry point for anyone who has always found traditional risotto too fussy to attempt on a Tuesday.
